nameStory: Micrasterias jenneri doesn't have a widely-used common name, but its scientific name tells a fascinating story. "Micrasterias" comes from Greek meaning "little star," perfectly describing these microscopic algae that look like intricate living snowflakes or tiny celestial bodies. The species was named "jenneri" to honor Edward Jenner, the famous English physician who developed the smallpox vaccine.
description: Micrasterias jenneri is a single-celled freshwater green alga that's invisible to the naked eye but absolutely stunning under a microscope. These tiny organisms are shaped like ornate stars or elaborate doilies, with intricate symmetrical patterns that would make any artist jealous. Each cell is typically about 100-200 micrometers across (that's smaller than the width of a human hair!) and consists of two mirror-image halves joined at the center. Despite being microscopic, they're some of the most beautiful and geometrically perfect organisms in New England's waters.

idTips.label: Star-like symmetry
idTips.description: Under a microscope, the cell appears as a perfect bilateral star with two identical halves that mirror each other across a central line, like a living Rorschach test

idTips.label: Deep lobing pattern
idTips.description: The cell edges are deeply divided into multiple rounded lobes or segments, creating an intricate lace-like appearance that's characteristic of this genus

idTips.label: Central constriction
idTips.description: A clear narrow waist or "isthmus" divides the two halves of the cell, often appearing as a bright line under the microscope

idTips.label: Smooth cell wall
idTips.description: The cell surface appears smooth and glassy under magnification, lacking the spines, warts, or other decorations found on some related species

idTips.label: Green coloration
idTips.description: Living cells appear bright green due to their chloroplasts, though the color may be faint due to their small size and transparency

habitat: You'll find Micrasterias jenneri floating in clean, slightly acidic freshwater environments like pristine ponds, quiet lake edges, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. They prefer soft water with low mineral content and are often found in areas with sphagnum moss or other bog plants. These microscopic beauties are indicators of good water quality and are most abundant in undisturbed aquatic habitats away from pollution.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin to increase as water temperatures warm and daylight hours lengthen, making this a good time to find them in pond samples.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm months when conditions are optimal for growth and reproduction. Water samples from quiet, shaded areas are most productive.
seasonality.fall: Numbers remain steady through early autumn, though populations may decline as temperatures cool and daylight decreases.
seasonality.winter: Populations persist but at much lower levels under ice cover. Some may form resting stages to survive harsh conditions.

funFact: Despite being single-celled organisms smaller than a grain of sand, Micrasterias jenneri cells can live for several weeks and actually "walk" across surfaces by secreting mucilage and changing their shape slightly, essentially crawling without any legs or muscles!
confusionNotes: Micrasterias jenneri can be confused with other members of its genus, but its relatively simple, smooth-edged lobes help distinguish it from the more ornate species like M. rotata (which has more pointed projections) or M. furcata (which has forked endings). Remember: jenneri has gentle, rounded lobes like a friendly star.
contextualKnowledge: These organisms belong to a group called desmids, which are among the most geometrically perfect life forms on Earth. Many people are surprised to learn that such intricate beauty exists in the microscopic world of pond water, and that these "living jewels" have been studied and admired by microscopists for over 150 years.
compareHints: Micrasterias jenneri differs from its relatives by having relatively simple, rounded lobes compared to the more elaborate projections of species like M. rotata or M. truncata. While M. americana tends to be larger and more robust, jenneri maintains a more delicate appearance with smoother margins. Unlike M. furcata which has distinctly forked or Y-shaped projections, jenneri's lobes remain undivided and gently curved.
